summary.title: Chapter 6 - Monitoring Distributed Systems
summary.one_liner: Learn Google SRE's principles for monitoring and alerting: what should page a human, symptoms versus causes, black-box versus white-box monitoring, and the four golden signals.
takeaways: Alerts that page a human should be actionable, urgent, and require intelligence; avoid noisy alerts that cause pager fatigue.
Monitor symptoms (what is broken) with more effort than causes (why), and only page on definite, imminent causes.
Use white-box monitoring for debugging and imminent problems, and black-box monitoring for active user-visible symptoms.
Measure the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) and track tail latency with histograms rather than means.
Keep monitoring simple; the Bigtable case study shows temporarily relaxing alerts to make long-term fixes.
summary.summary: This is Chapter 6 of the Google Site Reliability Engineering book, which sets out principles for building monitoring and alerting systems. It defines key terms such as monitoring, alerts, dashboards, root cause, and push, and explains why monitoring matters for trends, comparisons, alerting, dashboards, and debugging. It contrasts symptoms with causes, black-box with white-box monitoring, and gives the four golden signals along with guidance on tail latency, measurement resolution, and keeping systems simple. The chapter closes with a checklist for evaluating alerts and two case studies, Bigtable over-alerting and Gmail's human responses, which illustrate the long-term trade-offs.
